claims.text: Atom Probe Tomography can elucidate nanoprecipitate elemental redistribution during high-temperature oxidation of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
APT provides near-atomic-resolution, composition-sensitive profiling at precipitate–matrix interfaces.
Oxidation-driven segregation occurs at precipitate–matrix interfaces in this alloy.
The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy contains two distinct types of nanoprecipitates.
The matrix of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy is predominantly BCC.
Controlled oxidation at approximately 800–1000 °C in air is a suitable intervention for studying this alloy.
Controlled atmospheres with defined oxygen partial pressures can mimic relevant gas-turbine, power-plant, and aerospace service conditions.
Nanoprecipitates and their interfaces mediate elemental redistribution during oxidation.
Differential diffusion and oxidation kinetics cause element-specific segregation during high-temperature oxidation.
Cr or Ti may segregate at nanoprecipitate–matrix interfaces during oxidation.
Interfacial segregation alters local phase stability and oxide formation.
APT can detect oxidation-induced interfacial composition gradients at atomic scale.
Oxidized samples will exhibit significant interfacial segregation relative to unoxidized controls.
Local chemistry changes at nanoprecipitate boundaries are responsible for forming protective or less-protective oxide phases.
Thermogravimetric analysis is a bulk method suitable for measuring oxidation kinetics.
Conventional TEM/EDS mapping and bulk oxidation methods do not resolve atomic-scale composition gradients within nanoprecipitates.
Preparing representative APT specimens from oxidized material is challenging and may introduce artifacts.
APT quantification of light elements may be uncertain.
The correlation between nanoscale segregation profiles and overall oxidation rates may vary with temperature and exposure time.
Statistically indistinguishable APT composition profiles in oxidized and unoxidized samples would falsify the proposed oxidation-induced redistribution.
